analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage lenders to verify borrowers can repay and bans loan steering and prepayment penalties.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2009 with a single cosponsor, the bill died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to force creditors and mortgage brokers to verify — with tax returns, pay stubs, or bank records — that a borrower can actually afford a home loan's full payments, including taxes and insurance. It would ban steering borrowers into pricier loans than they qualify for, ban prepayment penalties, cap financed points and fees at 5% of the loan, require brokers to put the borrower's interest first, impose minimum financial standards on brokers, and require independent counseling before anyone refinances certain government-assisted or nonprofit mortgages. Reverse mortgages would be excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and homebuyers, especially lower- and middle-income borrowers. During the years leading up to the 2008 financial crisis, many loans were made with no check on whether the borrower could pay once teaser rates expired; this bill would have required documented income verification, tested affordability of adjustable-rate loans at a higher stress rate, and stopped brokers from steering people into more expensive products to earn bigger commissions. Borrowers refinancing government or nonprofit 'special mortgages' with unusual benefits would have to get independent counseling first, and the bill gives borrowers private legal remedies, including against investors who buy the loan.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders and brokers to verify a borrower's income with tax returns, payroll receipts, or bank records, and explicitly says a borrower's own statement of income is not enough.

Tests affordability of adjustable-rate loans at the fully indexed rate plus 200 basis points on a full-amortization schedule, so borrowers are qualified for the payment they will actually face later, not just the introductory payment.

Bars brokers and creditors from steering borrowers to loans more expensive than the ones they qualify for, bans mischaracterizing a borrower's credit history or a home's appraised value, and imposes a fiduciary-style duty to act in the borrower's best interest.
Prohibits prepayment penalties on home-secured loans and caps financed points, charges, and fees (including broker compensation from any source) at 5% of the loan principal.

Requires a $500,000 net worth or a $50,000 surety bond for mortgage brokers, and requires independent certification that a borrower received counseling before refinancing a government- or nonprofit-assisted mortgage with special payment benefits.

Gives borrowers a private cause of action for violations, lets them recover financed charges and unlawful broker compensation as damages, and extends liability to assignees and holders who buy the loan.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and lenders. They would bear the cost of full income documentation and stress-testing, lose income from prepayment penalties, steer-based compensation, and fees above the 5% cap, and face new lawsuits from borrowers. Small brokers unable to meet the $500,000 net worth or $50,000 bond requirement would have to leave the business. Lenders would also face assignee liability, meaning investors buying mortgages could be on the hook for origination violations.

drawbacks.text: A blanket prepayment penalty ban and a strict 5% cap on financed fees eliminate pricing tools some lenders used to offer lower upfront rates to borrowers short on cash at closing, which could raise closing costs for some creditworthy borrowers.
The $500,000 minimum net worth requirement would force many small, often locally based brokers out of the industry, reducing competition and choice in some markets.

Full documented income verification can slow closings and narrow access for borrowers with thin documentation, such as some self-employed or gig workers, and the bill excludes reverse mortgages, leaving seniors' loans out of its protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections address exactly the lending practices that produced mass foreclosures: undocumented income, teaser-rate loans qualified only at the introductory payment, steering, and prepayment penalties. The main costs fall on the mortgage industry, and the $500,000 net worth floor is the crudest part — it targets bad actors with a blunt capital requirement that would also eliminate small legitimate brokers. On balance the bill's core (ability to repay, anti-steering, fee caps) is well-aimed at borrower harm, with a real trade-off in market access for a minority of borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 30, 2009 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or markup and never reported it, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the Fairness for Homeowners Act of 2009 on March 30, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
That referral was the bill's last action of record; no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote ever occurred, and one Democrat cosponsored the bill.
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, with the bill still pending in committee, so it never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders, who avoided the origination standards, fee caps, and liability the bill would have imposed. Homebuyers stayed exposed to those practices until Congress wrote similar ability-to-repay and anti-steering rules into the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only members on record in support, the sponsor and its single cosponsor, were both Democrats, and the committee that never acted was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: Brokers would lose steering-based compensation, fees above a 5% cap, and prepayment penalty income, and would face a fiduciary duty to borrowers, new liability, and a $500,000 net worth or $50,000 bond requirement. Small brokers would be pushed out of the business entirely.

Lenders would have to document every borrower's ability to repay at a stress-tested payment and could face lawsuits and liability that follows the loan to any investor who buys it, raising origination costs and litigation risk.
HUD-certified or state-certified nonprofit counselors would gain a required role: independent certification before any refinancing of government- or nonprofit-assisted 'special mortgages.'
